justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift over time, anchored around a current level near 37.3. For the one-day horizon, I anchored heavily on the most recent observed value, expecting minimal movement given typical short-term mean-reversion and low intraday volatility in whatever underlying series this represents. For the one-week estimate, I nudged the value slightly higher to 37.4, reflecting a gentle positive trend bias while acknowledging that weekly fluctuations tend to average out near recent levels. For the one-month estimate, I extended that drift to 37.6, incorporating a slow secular trend while recognizing that a month is long enough for genuine directional movement to accumulate, though the central tendency still gravitates toward recent realized values.

The confidence interval widths reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only 1.6 units (36.5 to 38.1), consistent with the relatively bounded day-to-day variation one typically observes in stable time series. At one week, the interval widens to 3.2 units (35.8 to 39.0), capturing the possibility of a few consecutive moves in the same direction or an unexpected shock. At one month, the interval expands to 6.2 units (34.5 to 40.7), reflecting that over four weeks, structural shifts, external shocks, or regime changes become meaningfully more likely. The width progression roughly follows a square-root-of-time scaling, which is a standard assumption when volatility is approximately constant and returns are roughly independent across periods.

There are several risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden negative shock — whether a macroeconomic announcement, policy change, or data revision — could push the series well below 34.5 within a month. On the upside, a sustained positive catalyst or an unexpected acceleration in whatever underlying trend is present could carry the value above 40.7. Additionally, my intervals assume relative stability in the data-generating process, so any structural break — a change in measurement methodology, a market regime shift, or an extraordinary external event — would render these bounds too narrow. The one-day interval is most vulnerable to being breached by a single large discrete jump that I have not explicitly modeled.
